records.place: Villanova di Farra, Farra d'Isonzo, Venezia Giulia IGT, Friuli Venezia Giulia

wine.name: Vintage Tunina
wine.classification: Venezia Giulia IGT, the regional tier below DOC, by the house's choice
wine.grapes: Sauvignon and Chardonnay with Ribolla Gialla and Malvasia, and for many years a little Picolit; the mix follows the vintage.
wine.sites: The Tunina vineyard at Ronco del Fortino, on hill soils of marl and sandstone of Eocene origin, where the varieties grow together as one field blend.
wine.making: The varieties grow together and are picked together late, about two weeks after the usual harvest; accounts differ on whether they then ferment as one or apart. The wine rests on its fine lees for longer than is usual before bottling. It saw no wood in the 1990s; some later vintages have had a part raised in large oak.
wine.glass: Ripe pear, acacia honey and wildflowers over salted almond and a little peach, with a touch of vanilla in the years that see oak; broad and textured, yet fresh, with a long almond finish.
wine.ageing: Open and generous on release; by the house's account it keeps seven or eight years, and longer than ten in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 11 to 13 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass with a generous bowl.

label.means: The wine's name: Vintage is part of the name, and the year beside it is the harvest.
The regional IGT of Friuli Venezia Giulia, freer than a DOC in the grapes it allows.

records.table: Jermann's Vintage Tunina is the white blend of Villanova di Farra, first sold with the 1975: a field of Sauvignon, Chardonnay and native grapes grown together and picked late together. Pear, acacia honey and salted almond, broad yet fresh; pour it cool, never icy.
records.story: The family came to Villanova di Farra in 1881, when its founder settled there from Burgenland in Austria, as the house tells it, and the Jermanns farmed there for generations. In the early 1970s a descendant who had trained at the wine schools of Conegliano and San Michele, and studied abroad for a time, set out to make a white of several varieties grown together in one vineyard and picked late together. The trials began with the 1973 harvest, and the first wine sold as Vintage Tunina was the 1975. The name is that of the vineyard at Ronco del Fortino; as the house tells it, the name recalls a former owner called Antonia, Tunina in the local diminutive, and the story links it to a Venetian housekeeper of that name loved by Giacomo Casanova (1725 to 1798). The wine is bottled under the regional IGT, outside the DOC, by the house's choice, and for many years it carried a little Picolit. In 2021 a majority of the estate passed to Marchesi Antinori. For a sommelier Vintage Tunina is where the Friulian white blend starts: several grapes, one field, and texture rather than the voice of a single variety.

others.name: Vinnae
others.note: The house's white led by Ribolla Gialla, the native grape of the Gorizia hills, with a little Friulano and Riesling.

others.name: Capo Martino
others.note: A white blend led by Friulano and raised in wood.

traps: Vintage Tunina is a field blend of several grapes, never a varietal wine, and Vintage is part of its name rather than a vintage designation.
It is labelled Venezia Giulia IGT, not Collio DOC or Friuli Isonzo DOC, by the house's choice.
Jermann's Ribolla led white is Vinnae; Vintage Tunina carries Ribolla only as one part of its blend.

cards.front: Jermann's Vintage Tunina: which harvest gave the first trials, and which wine was the first sold under the name?
cards.back: The 1973 harvest gave the trials; the 1975 was the first sold as Vintage Tunina.

cards.front: Whose name, the story goes, does the Tunina vineyard of Jermann recall?
cards.back: Antonia, called Tunina, a former owner, and a Venetian housekeeper of that name loved by Casanova.

questions.q: A guest asks when the grapes for Jermann's Vintage Tunina are picked. Which answer fits?
opts: Late, about two weeks after the usual harvest
Early, before the usual harvest, for freshness
In midwinter, frozen on the vine
Early, then dried for months on mats
questions.exp: The house picks the Tunina vineyard late, about two weeks after the usual harvest, for ripeness and texture; the grapes are neither picked early nor dried or frozen.

questions.q: After trials of the 1973 harvest, which vintage was the first Jermann sold under the name Vintage Tunina?
questions.exp: The house dates the trials to the 1973 harvest and the first wine sold under the name to the 1975; 1981 is the first vintage of Livio Felluga's Terre Alte, another Friulian blend.

sources.title: Decanter: Wine Legend, Jermann Vintage Tunina 1997
Decanter: Antinori expands into Friuli white wines with Jermann deal
Gambero Rosso International: Antinori acquires the majority of the Jermann winery

report: Seven searches of my own (two on the house's domain for its history and the Tunina factsheet, one on Decanter's domain, four open) and one WebFetch of Decanter refused by the network and not retried.

Founded 1881 rests on the house's own pages (the founder from Burgenland, one page by way of Bilijana in Slovenia; the pages disagree whether he was the great grandfather or a more distant forebear of the man who made Tunina), so he is described, his dates not found; the library leaves founded empty.

The house's factsheet lists Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Ribolla Gialla and Malvasia, while Decanter's 1997 profile and merchants add Picolit, so the grapes give a little Picolit in many years; the library's w-vintage-tunina lists Picolit as a fixed part.

The making rests on Decanter (picked and fermented together, whole bunch pressing, long lees, no wood in the 1990s and some oak since) and one merchant (a part in large wood); no fermentation vessel was found on the house's pages, so none is named.

The Casanova link is told as a story on Decanter's account, the house's page naming only the vineyard; Gambero Rosso's wine of the year for the 1997 rests on Decanter and a merchant (announced in November 1999), and the integrator may cut it if a guide's award reads as a rating.
Antinori's majority of 2021 rests on Decanter and Gambero Rosso; the Ruttars cellar of 2007 and the house's Chardonnay under a song title were left out for want of a second source.

The glass rests on the library (ripe pear, acacia, salted almond), Decanter (acacia honey) and merchants' notes (wildflowers, peach, vanilla in oaked years); the keeping of seven to eight years, more than ten in a strong year, is the house's factsheet.

changed: wine.making: was pressed as whole bunches and fermented together; now picked together late with the accounts said to differ on fermenting as one or apart, since Decanter has a field blend fermented together while a review of the 2022 has the grapes fermented apart and a merchant's sheet of the 2023 has steel with part finished in large oak; whole bunch pressing rested on one source and is cut.
wine.grapes: was Malvasia Istriana and in many years a little Picolit; now Malvasia, as the house's factsheet prints it, and for many years a little Picolit, as the house's Picolit page tells it.

wine.sites: was the Tunina vineyard in Villanova di Farra on the Eocene flysch of the Gorizia hills; now Ronco del Fortino on hill soils of marl and sandstone of Eocene origin, since the accounts place the vineyard in the heart of the Collio or near Gorizia and none read placed it in Villanova di Farra.
wine.label: the term Indicazione Geografica Tipica is cut, since merchants list recent bottles as IGP and the words in full were not confirmed on the label.
table and story: was picked late together and fermented as one; now grown together and picked late together.

story: the guide's wine of the year for the 1997 is cut, a guide's award being a rating; worked abroad is now studied abroad for a time, the house's research sabbatical overseas; the Casanova link is told as the house tells it; the majority of 2021 is told as passing to Marchesi Antinori; the Picolit of many years is added.

others[0], traps[1] and traps[2]: Vinnae is now a white led by Ribolla Gialla with a little Friulano and Riesling, as merchants' sheets of several vintages give it; the trap no longer places the vineyard in the Gorizia hills.

questions: the wine question's key of grapes fermented as one gave way to a question on the late harvest, two weeks after the usual one by the house's own pages; the story question's 1997 distractor and its guide award are replaced by 1971 and Terre Alte's 1981.
open: Whether the varieties ferment together or apart, and the share of oak in recent vintages, stay unsettled; a house news page of 2017 speaks of the traditional method of ageing the wine in cement vats, which no other source repeats.
The founder, Anton Jermann by the house and merchants, is described, his dates not found; 1881 is the house's year of his arrival, kept as the founding, with the library's founded empty.
The exact place of Ronco del Fortino was not settled: one account has it in the heart of the Collio, another near Gorizia; the house says only that the grapes come from it.
One merchant ties the name Tunina to a daughter of the family; the house's account of a former owner and Casanova's housekeeper is kept.

records.place: Brazzano di Cormòns, vineyards at Rosazzo, Rosazzo DOCG, Friuli Venezia Giulia

wine.name: Terre Alte
wine.classification: DOCG since 2011, a white blend led by Friulano from the Rosazzo hills
wine.grapes: Friulano, at least half as the Rosazzo DOCG requires, with Pinot Bianco and Sauvignon for the rest.
wine.sites: The house's hill vineyards at Rosazzo, round the old abbey south of Cividale, on the marl and sandstone of Eocene origin called ponca.
wine.making: Picked by hand into small crates, the grapes are lightly destemmed, left briefly on their skins and gently pressed. The settled must begins its fermentation in stainless steel and moves to oak casks, where it finishes fermenting and goes through malolactic. It then stays on its lees for savour and length, and is bottled in the summer.
wine.glass: Pear and hay over acacia and hawthorn blossom, with almond, wild herbs and crushed stone; full and creamy from the lees, with fresh acidity and a long, saline finish.
wine.ageing: Ready on release, it gains depth and the tertiary notes of age over the years that follow in bottle, as the house means it to.
wine.serve: 11 to 13 degrees Celsius; no need to decant, though it opens in a large glass; a white Burgundy glass.

label.means: The DOCG of 2011 for white blends of at least half Friulano, from the hills round the abbey of Rosazzo.
Italian for high lands: the name of the blend first made with the 1981 vintage.

label.term: Denominazione di Origine Controllata e Garantita
label.means: DOCG: Italy's guaranteed appellation, its rules set by decree.

records.table: Livio Felluga's Terre Alte is the white blend of the Rosazzo hills, first made in 1981: Friulano with Pinot Bianco and Sauvignon, begun in steel, finished in oak casks and kept on its lees. Pear, acacia and almond with a saline finish; pour it cool in a large glass.
records.story: Livio Felluga (1914 to 2016) was born at Isola d'Istria, then part of Austria-Hungary, and settled at the foot of the Rosazzo hills at the end of the 1930s, before the war took him to the front. After the war he bought vineyards on the hill of Rosazzo, round its old abbey, and he founded the house at Brazzano in 1956. That year, by the house's account, he conceived a label printed with an old map of the Friulian hills, to say where the wine came from in the years before Italy had DOCs, and the map has marked the house's wines ever since. Terre Alte followed with the 1981 vintage: Friulano, Pinot Bianco and Sauvignon from the Rosazzo hills, made as one wine rather than three. In 2011 Rosazzo, until then a subzone of the Colli Orientali, became a DOCG for white blends of at least half Friulano, and Terre Alte is labelled under it. Livio Felluga died at his home in Brazzano in December 2016, at the age of 102, and his family carried the house on. For a sommelier Terre Alte and the map say the same thing: the hill comes first and the grapes serve it.

others.name: Friulano
others.note: The house's single variety Friulano of the Colli Orientali, the regional grape in its plain form.

others.name: Picolit
others.note: The sweet white of the shy native Picolit grape, from the Colli Orientali.

traps: Terre Alte is a blend led by Friulano, not a varietal Friulano; the house bottles its Friulano on its own.
Rosazzo is a DOCG within the Friuli Colli Orientali hills of the province of Udine, not part of the Collio, though the Felluga cellar stands at Brazzano by Cormòns.

cards.front: Livio Felluga: what has the house printed on its labels since 1956?
cards.back: An old map of the Friulian hills, to show where the wine comes from.

cards.front: Terre Alte: which DOCG does it carry, and which grape must lead the blend?
cards.back: Rosazzo DOCG, created in 2011; Friulano must make at least half the blend.

questions.q: Under the Rosazzo DOCG that Livio Felluga's Terre Alte carries, which grape must make at least half the blend?
questions.exp: The Rosazzo rules ask for at least half Friulano, with Sauvignon and Pinot Bianco or Chardonnay each a fifth to three tenths; Ribolla Gialla may add no more than a tenth.

questions.q: With which vintage was Livio Felluga's Terre Alte first made?
questions.exp: Terre Alte was born with the 1981 vintage; 1956 is the year of the map label and 2011 the year Rosazzo became a DOCG.

sources.title: MMD USA: Livio Felluga, the story

report: Six searches of my own (one on the house's domain, five open), no WebFetch tried.

Livio Felluga's dates: born in 1914 at Isola d'Istria by two producer profiles, dead at Brazzano in December 2016 at 102 by Dissapore, an Italian news report and a merchant's profile, one giving the night of 21 to 22 December.

The map label of 1956 rests on an importer's and a merchant's account and the library's founding year; the house's own history page says only that he set up the cellar at Brazzano and bought the first Rosazzo vineyards in the 1950s.

One merchant gave Sauvignon 40 and Friulano and Pinot Bianco 30 each for an older vintage, which the Rosazzo DOCG's rule of at least half Friulano would not allow, so the grapes give the rule and no figure; a house page listing a wider blend with Malvasia Istriana and Ribolla Gialla was not taken for Terre Alte.

The making is the house's own page (steel, then oak casks for the end of fermentation and the malolactic, lees, a summer bottling); older accounts of Sauvignon alone in barrique were not found and are not given.

The year Terre Alte moved from Colli Orientali del Friuli Rosazzo Bianco to the Rosazzo DOCG label was not found, so the story says only that it is labelled under it; Gambero Rosso's account of an idea of the founder's sons in the late 1970s is one source and left out.
data-advanced's question has Terre Alte make the Rosazzo DOCG famous; no source for that was sought and the record does not claim it.
The glass rests on the library (pear, hay, almond, saline) and Falstaff's notes (acacia, hawthorn, wild herbs, crushed stone), Falstaff not cited for want of room.

changed: story: was came to the Friulian hills in the 1930s and in the 1950s set up a cellar at Brazzano and bought his first vineyards; now settled at the foot of the Rosazzo hills at the end of the 1930s before the war took him to the front, bought vineyards on the hill after the war and founded the house at Brazzano in 1956, as Felluga's profiles by Callmewine, Lea and Sandeman and the importer tell it.
story: the map label is now conceived in 1956 by the house's account, in the years before Italy had DOCs, as the house's own site and the Messaggero Veneto's obituary by way of Dissapore tell it.
story: Rosazzo is now told as a subzone of the Colli Orientali until it became a DOCG in 2011, by the decree of 14 October 2011.
wine.sites: the Cappuccina training cut, since no search found it for Felluga's Rosazzo vines.
open: The year Terre Alte moved from Colli Orientali del Friuli Rosazzo Bianco to the Rosazzo DOCG label was not found.
The glass rests on the library and the author's Falstaff notes; no tasting note of the house's own was read.

records.place: Capriva del Friuli, Collio DOC, Friuli Venezia Giulia

wine.name: Collio Friulano
wine.classification: DOC Collio Goriziano or Collio, the hill zone of Gorizia province, since 1968
wine.grapes: Friulano alone, the grape once labelled Tocai Friulano.
wine.sites: The house's hill vineyards at Capriva del Friuli, round the Archbishop's palace whose vines the Church leased to the founder, on marly soils of Eocene origin.
wine.making: Fermented for ten to twelve days in stainless steel at a controlled 16 degrees Celsius, the wine rests eight months on its lees in steel, with no wood, and then at least five months in bottle before release.
wine.glass: Pear and pear skin with white blossom and a little almond, ending on the grape's bitter almond note; medium bodied, clean and precise, with fresh acidity and no oak.
wine.ageing: Fresh and open on release, it keeps and deepens for some years in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass of medium size.

label.means: The DOC of the Gorizia hills along the Slovenian border, on the marl and sandstone called ponca.
The grape sold as Tocai Friulano until the name Tocai was withdrawn in the EU from 2007.
DOC: Italy's controlled appellation, below DOCG, its rules set by decree.

records.table: Schiopetto's Collio Friulano comes from the Capriva hills: Friulano alone, first made in 1965, fermented cool in steel and kept eight months on its lees with no wood. Pear, white blossom and a bitter almond finish; pour it with prosciutto di San Daniele.
records.story: Mario Schiopetto (1930 to 2003) first worked in his family's inn before he turned to wine. He travelled to cellars across Europe, in Germany above all for the making of white wine and in France for finesse. He began making wine in 1963 and released his first Tocai, a single variety white, in 1965, by the house's account. He was among the first in Friuli to ferment white wine in stainless steel under temperature control, for freshness and clean varietal aroma, and his cold, clean whites became the pattern of the region's modern style. The Church leased him the vineyards round the Archbishop's palace at Capriva, from 1970 by the house's account, though another account dates the lease to 1965; he restored them, and in 1989 they became his own. He died in 2003 at seventy two, and his children carried on. In 2007 the name Tocai was withdrawn in the EU, to protect Hungary's Tokaj, and the wine became Friulano on the label. In April 2014 the estate passed to new owners, who undertook to keep its style. For a sommelier this Friulano marks where the modern Friulian white began: one variety, no wood, nothing between the grape and the glass.

others.name: Collio Pinot Bianco
others.note: Pinot Bianco alone from the Collio hills, first produced in 1967 by the house's sheets.

others.name: Blanc des Rosis
others.note: The house's white blend led by Friulano, raised like the Friulano for eight months on its lees in steel.

traps: Friulano and Tocai Friulano are one grape: the name Tocai was withdrawn from 2007, and the grape has nothing to do with Hungary's Tokaji.
Schiopetto's Friulano is the clean, steel made pole of Friulian white; the skin macerated orange wines of Oslavia are a separate and later movement.

cards.front: Schiopetto: in which year did the house release its first Tocai, the wine later labelled Friulano?
cards.back: 1965, two years after its founder began making wine, by the house's account.

cards.front: How is Schiopetto's Collio Friulano raised before release?
cards.back: Eight months on its lees in stainless steel, with no wood, then at least five months in bottle.

questions.q: A guest asks whether Schiopetto's Collio Friulano sees oak. What is the answer?
opts: No: steel throughout, eight months on its lees
Yes: a year in new French barriques
Partly: a third in large Slavonian casks
Yes: months in buried clay amphorae
questions.exp: The house ferments and raises its Friulano in stainless steel, eight months on the lees, then bottles it; barriques and amphorae belong to other Friulian cellars.

questions.q: From whom did Mario Schiopetto first lease the Capriva vineyards that became his own in 1989?
opts: The Church, round the Archbishop's palace
The commune of Capriva del Friuli
questions.exp: The Church leased him the vineyards round the Archbishop's palace at Capriva, and he restored them and made them his own in 1989; no commune, cooperative or merchant held them.

sources.title: Decanter: Father of Friuli Schiopetto dies
Grandi Bottiglie: Mario Schiopetto producer page

report: Six searches of my own (two on the house's domain, one on Decanter's and DiWineTaste's, three open), no WebFetch beyond the Decanter host already refused.

Mario Schiopetto's dates: born in 1930 by the house's own pages, dead at seventy two by Decanter's obituary and in 2003 by Callmewine's profile; the obituary's own date was not shown, so the checker may confirm 2003.

The house's pages disagree on the start: the home page has wine from 1963 and the first Tocai of 1965, the history page has the story begin in 1970 with the Church's lease (the vineyards bought in 1989), and Decanter has bottling from 1964; the record keeps the library's 1965 and tells both.

Among the first in Friuli to ferment white wine in stainless steel under temperature control rests on Grandi Bottiglie and a German merchant's profile; the library's p-schiopetto says he brought temperature control to Italy, a first for the whole country that no source read confirmed.
The sale of April 2014 is the house's own history; the buyers are a living family and are not named.
The library's Collio Friulano note calls it a benchmark, a judgement word, and its Pinot Bianco note a quiet triumph; neither is used.
The inn's name, the Osteria ai Pompieri in Udine, and his father's name rest on Vinous alone and are left out.

changed: story: was in 1970 the Church leased him the vineyards; now from 1970 by the house's account, though another account dates the lease to 1965, since Superiore has rented vines from the Archbishop of Gorizia from 1965 and the house's history begins in 1970.
wine.sites and questions[1]: the year 1970 is taken out of the sites and of the question's stem, so the question has one right answer whichever year holds.

table: was as the house has made its white since 1965; now first made in 1965, since the house's sheet of the 2019 gives the eight months on the lees in steel and no source gave the making of the 1960s.
others[1]: was a white blend in the manner of a field blend; now led by Friulano and raised eight months on its lees in steel, as the house's own page gives it.
open: His start in 1963 rests on the house's home page as the author read it; Decanter has bottling from 1964.
The sale of April 2014 rests on the house's history and two merchants' profiles; the buying family is living and not named.

records.place: Oslavia, Gorizia, Venezia Giulia IGT, Friuli Venezia Giulia

wine.name: Ribolla Gialla
wine.classification: Venezia Giulia IGT, the regional tier, chosen in place of the Collio DOC
wine.grapes: Ribolla Gialla alone, the native white grape of the Collio, grown as Rebula across the Slovenian border.
wine.sites: The family's hill vineyards at Oslavia on the Slovenian border, on the marl and sandstone of the Collio; the house's own pages record a planting of Ribolla at Hum in 1996.
wine.making: Fermented with wild yeasts in Georgian clay amphorae buried in the ground, the wine stays on its skins for about six months. Pressed, it returns to amphora for some months more, then rests for years in large casks of Slavonian oak, about six as a rule, and leaves the cellar some seven years after the harvest.
wine.glass: Amber in the glass: dried apricot, orange peel and acacia honey over beeswax, resin, tea leaf and roasted almond; dry and deep, with a fine grip of tannin, fresh acidity and long, savoury length.
wine.ageing: Released about seven years after the vintage and ready to drink then, it keeps for many years more in a cool cellar.
wine.serve: 14 to 16 degrees Celsius, cellar cool and never chilled, warmer if it seems closed; open it an hour ahead or decant it, as the aromas open with air; a large white Burgundy glass.

label.means: The grape as the house prints it: Ribolla Gialla in full, Rebula across the Slovenian border.
The regional IGT under which the house bottles its wines rather than as Collio DOC.

records.table: Gravner's Ribolla Gialla is the orange wine of Oslavia: a white grape fermented on its skins for months in Georgian amphorae buried in the earth, then aged years in large oak. Amber, with apricot, honey, tea and a grip of tannin; pour it cool, never cold.
records.story: By its own account the family bought its house at Oslavia, on the hill above Gorizia, with a little land, in 1901. In the 1980s the son of the house modernised the cellar with stainless steel tanks and French barriques. He came to distrust that style. When hail in 1996 destroyed most of the Ribolla crop, he macerated what survived on its skins, and the long maceration became the house's way. A journey to Georgia in 2000 showed him the qvevri, clay jars buried in the earth, and the first of them arrived at Oslavia in 2001; clay took over the cellar in the years that followed. Early in the 2010s the vines of grapes from elsewhere were pulled up, leaving Ribolla and the native red Pignolo. The wines are bottled as Venezia Giulia IGT rather than as Collio DOC, and each leaves the cellar some seven years after its harvest. For a sommelier this Ribolla is where the story of Italian orange wine is told from: a white grape made like a red, then given years of patience before anyone pours it.

others.name: Bianco Breg
others.note: A white blend of Chardonnay, Sauvignon, Pinot Grigio and Riesling Italico made the same way, until those vines were pulled up early in the 2010s.

others.name: Rosso Gravner
others.note: A red, Merlot with a small part of another grape by the house's sheet for the 2010, fermented in amphora and raised for years in Slavonian oak.

traps: Ribolla Gialla is a white grape: the amber colour comes from months on the skins, not from red grapes or from age alone.
Gravner bottles as Venezia Giulia IGT, not Collio DOC, though its vines stand in the Collio hills.
Radikon, its neighbour at Oslavia, macerates in large oak vats; the buried Georgian amphorae are Gravner's.

cards.front: Gravner: what happened in 1996 that turned its Ribolla towards long skin contact?
cards.back: Hail destroyed most of the Ribolla crop, and what survived was macerated on its skins.

cards.front: Where did the clay vessels of Gravner's Ribolla come from, and in which year did the first arrive?
cards.back: From Georgia, after a journey there in 2000; the first arrived at Oslavia in 2001.

questions.q: About how long does Gravner's Ribolla Gialla stay on its skins in amphora?
questions.exp: The Ribolla macerates about six months on its skins in buried amphorae before pressing; eight days was the skin contact Radikon, its neighbour, gave its wines in 1997.

questions.q: From which country did Gravner import the buried clay jars it first brought to Oslavia in 2001?
questions.exp: After a journey to Georgia in 2000 the first qvevri arrived in 2001; the tinajas of Spain and the talhas of Portugal are other clay traditions.

report: Six searches of my own (one on the house's domain, one on Decanter's, four open), no WebFetch tried; founded is left empty, as in the library, because the house's 1901 is the purchase of the Oslavia house, not a founding.
The grower is living and never named; the library's p-gravner carries his name as its producer name (Josko Gravner), as do data-advanced and data-cms.

The timeline rests on Decanter's producer profile and Primal Wine (hail in 1996, Georgia in 2000, the first amphorae for the 2001 vintage); the steel and barriques of the 1980s rest on two Decanter pieces, and the visit to California of 1987, the barriques gone in 1999 and the whole cellar in amphora by 2005 on Decanter alone, so those three are left out.

The region record has Oslavia move Ribolla into buried Georgian amphorae from the late 1990s; the skin contact dates from 1996 and the amphorae from the 2001 vintage, so the library's from 2001 and the question bank's 2001 vintage hold and the region line is loose.
The library's Rosso Gravner is Pignolo, but the house's own sheet for Rosso Gravner 2010 gives Merlot with a small part of another grape, so the record says mostly Merlot.
The house's product list prints the wine as Ribolla, so wine.name keeps the plan's Ribolla Gialla and the label term gives Ribolla; the integrator may prefer the plan's wine to read Ribolla.

Sources give six to seven months on the skins and up to eight years to release, so the record says about six months and some seven years; a drinking glass of the grower's own design was searched for and not confirmed.

changed: wine.making: no temperature control is cut, for want of a second source; about six years in large oak is now about six as a rule, since the International Wine Challenge reports that the house ordered glass tanks in 2024 to take part of that time.

wine.serve: was 12 to 14 degrees Celsius; now 14 to 16, cellar cool and warmer if closed, since Decanter advises serving Gravner and Radikon close to room temperature after a first taste at 12 to 14 and merchants give 14 to 16 and 16 to 18.

story: was hail left only a small part of the crop; now destroyed most of the Ribolla crop, ninety five per cent by Decanter; was the first amphorae for the 2001 vintage and from then on the whites fermented in clay; now the first arrived in 2001 and clay took over in the years that followed, since Decanter has the whole cellar in amphora only by 2005.

story and others[0]: was the vines of grapes from elsewhere pulled up in 2012; now early in the 2010s, since one account has the last Breg in 2012 and a merchant quoting the estate 2011; Breg's grapes are now named, Chardonnay, Sauvignon, Pinot Grigio and Riesling Italico.
others[1]: Rosso Gravner is now Merlot with a small part of another grape by the house's sheet for the 2010, as the sheet's own title gives it, rather than mostly Merlot without a vintage.

records.place: Oslavia, Gorizia, Venezia Giulia IGT, Friuli Venezia Giulia

wine.name: Oslavje
wine.classification: Venezia Giulia IGT, the regional tier, used in place of the Collio DOC
wine.grapes: Chardonnay, Sauvignon and Pinot Grigio, as the house first made it in 1992; merchants list later vintages as Chardonnay and Sauvignon alone.
wine.sites: The family's hill vineyards at Oslavia, neighbouring Gravner's on the Slovenian border, on the marl and sandstone of the Collio hills.
wine.making: Fermented with wild yeasts in large oak vats, the wine stays about three months on its skins, as every wine of the house has since 2002. It then rests three years or more in large casks of Slavonian oak and a year or two in bottle, and goes out with no sulphur added.
wine.glass: Deep amber: dried apricot, orange peel and cider apple over walnut, wild herbs and tea leaf, with a little honey; dry, with chewy tannin, bright acidity and a long, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Released some four or five years after the vintage and ready then, it keeps for many years and gains depth in bottle.
wine.serve: 14 to 16 degrees Celsius, cellar cool and never chilled, warmer if it seems closed; open it an hour ahead or decant it, as the aromas open with air; a large white Burgundy glass.

label.means: The Slovene name of Oslavia, the hamlet above Gorizia where the vines grow.
The regional IGT of Friuli Venezia Giulia, used here in place of the Collio DOC.

records.table: Radikon's Oslavje is an orange wine of Oslavia: Chardonnay and Sauvignon, with Pinot Grigio in its early years, kept about three months on their skins in oak vats, then aged years in large Slavonian casks with no sulphur added. Amber, apricot and orange peel; serve it cool.
records.story: The vines at Oslavia were first planted by the grandfather of the man who made the estate's name, who grew Ribolla for the family's own wine. His grandson took on the vineyards in the late 1970s and bottled the estate's first wines from the 1979 vintage, as the house records. Oslavje followed in 1992, a blend of Chardonnay, Sauvignon and Pinot Grigio named with the hamlet's Slovene name. In 1995, the turning point in the house's own words, he macerated his Ribolla on its skins, and from 1997 Oslavje had the same treatment, at first for about eight days. By 2002 every wine spent about three months on its skins and went into bottle with no sulphur added; the house also moved to a new cork and to bottles of half a litre and a litre. He died on 11 September 2016, and his son carried the estate on. For a sommelier Oslavje shows the Oslavia way with grapes from elsewhere: grapes such as Chardonnay and Sauvignon made like a red wine, in wood rather than clay, and kept long before release.

report: Seven searches of my own (three on the house's domain, four open), no WebFetch tried; the respelling is left empty, the stress of the name not confirmed.

The man who made the estate's name died on 11 September 2016 by Decanter and the house's memorial page, at 62 by Decanter and 61 by RTV Slovenija; his birth year was not found in two sources, so he is described and never named, and his son is living and not named.

The grandfather, Franz Mikulus in two importers' profiles, is described, his dates not found; the family on the hill since 1861 and the parents' commercial start of 1948 rest on one profile each and are left out.

The house's history gives Oslavje of 1992 as Pinot Grigio, Sauvignon and Chardonnay; importers list later bottlings as Chardonnay and Sauvignon, Pinot Grigio moved to a wine of its own, which the house's pages did not confirm, so the grapes hedge.

The making: two to three months on the skins, three years in barrel and one to two in bottle by the house's sheet; open oak vats, wild yeasts and large Slavonian casks by Bowler and Dynamic Vines; no temperature control by one merchant.
The half litre and litre bottles rest on the house's timeline, Palate Press, merchants' listings and the library; a new neck and cork of the grower's design was not confirmed and is left out.

changed: wine.making: was two to three months on the skins in open oak vats with no temperature control, about three years in large casks, unfiltered; now about three months in large oak vats as every wine since 2002 by the house's timeline, three years or more in large Slavonian casks by an importer and a merchant, with no temperature control and unfiltered cut for want of a second source.
wine.serve: was 12 to 14 degrees Celsius; now 14 to 16, cellar cool and warmer if closed, by Decanter's advice for Radikon and Gravner.
table: open oak vats and two to three months now oak vats and about three months.

story: was the first wine of the 1979 vintage; now the first wines, since the house lists five wines of the 1979 bottled in 1980; as his grandfather had done is cut, one account only; the new cork of 2002 is added from the house's timeline.
traps[1]: was Radikon bottles in half litre and litre sizes; now Oslavje and the other long macerated wines, since the house's other lines were not checked.
open: The year Pinot Grigio left Oslavje rests on merchants' listings; the house's pages give only the blend of 1992.
A year or two in bottle and the wild yeasts rest on the author's reading of the house's sheet and two importers, not reached again.
The respelling stays empty; the stress of the name was not confirmed.
